fetched_contents.text: Effects of parasitic freshwater mussels on their host fishes: a review ---------------------------------------- Key words: Conservation, freshwater mussel, glochidia, host effects, Unionida Abstract Freshwater mussels in the order Unionida are highly adapted to parasitize fish for the primary purpose of dispersal. The parasitic larval stage affixes itself to the gills or fins of the host where it becomes encysted in the tissue, eventually excysting to develop into a free-living adult. Research on the parasitic interactions between unionids and their host fishes has garnered attention recently due to the increase in worldwide preservation efforts surrounding this highly endangered and ecologically significant order. With the exception of heavy infestation events, these mussels cause minor effects to their hosts, typically only observable effect in combination with other stressors. Moreover, the range of effect intensities on the host varies greatly with the species involved in the interaction, an effect that may arise from different evolutionary strategies between long- and short-infesting mussels; a distinction not typically made in conservation practices. Lower growth and reduced osmotic potential in infested hosts are commonly observed and correlated with infestation load. These effects are typically also associated with increases in metabolic rate and behaviour indicative of stress. Host fish seem to compensate for this through a combination of rapid wound healing in the parasitized areas and higher ventilation rates. The findings are heavily biased towards Margaritifera margaritifera, a unique mussel not well suited for cross-species generalizations. Furthermore, the small body of molecular and genetic studies should be expanded as many conclusions are drawn from studies on the ultimate effects of glochidiosis rather than proximate studies on the underlying mechanisms. Introduction The relationships between parasites and their hosts are among the most complex and specialized forms of organism interactions on the planet. Interest in these interactions has grown rapidly since the inclusion of parasitology to the field of evolutionary ecology, as parasites have been shown to play a key role in regulating population size (Scott and Dobson, 1989; Tompkins et al., 2002), behaviour (Wesołowska and Wesołowski, 2014) and the general ecology of hosts (Poulin and FitzGerald, 1989), as well as shaping evolution (Rook, 2007; Parratt and Laine, 2016). For example, parasites have even been proposed as a driving factor behind the evolution of sexual reproduction (Hamilton et al., 1990). Perhaps the most widely accepted definition of the term parasite is ‘an organism that lives in or on another organism, the host, and causes it some harm by exploiting it through a structurally adapted way of life’ (Poulin, 2007). This definition can be applied to plants, fungi, animals, viruses, bacteria and, some argue, even to specific DNA strands (Combes, 2000, 2001; Poulin, 2007). The term parasite has also been described in an ecological sense as ‘predators that eat prey units of less than one’ (Wilson, 2014). Given the vast diversity of parasitic organisms, the literature typically categorizes them according to the strategies that they have evolved. Among the factors taken into account when describing a parasite are the location on the host which the parasite infests, the number of hosts the parasite requires to complete its life cycle and the proportion of the life cycle spent as a parasite (Box 1). Parasites have been generally regarded as negative factors in healthy ecosystems and are regularly the target of eradication efforts. However, arguments against the widespread eradication of parasites have begun to emerge (Marcogliese, 2004). Firstly, in cases where parasitic infestation is common within a population, hosts have likely evolved mechanisms to tolerate it. The effects caused by, or induced from, the infestation may play a role in the normal functioning of the host immune system or physiological processes, the lack of which may lead to deleterious effects in the host (Rook, 2007; Flohr et al., 2009; Pizzi, 2009). As the survival of a parasite is often dependent on the (temporary) survival of the host, it is not always advantageous for the parasite to significantly affect host survival (Poulin, 2007). Secondly, as parasites have effects on host tissue, host behaviour or both, increases or decreases in parasite abundance can have significant downstream effects on both biotic and abiotic aspects of the ecosystem (Mouritsen and Poulin, 2003, 2005). As an example, parasite-induced trophic transmission (PITT), also known as trophic facilitation, is a commonly, but not ubiquitously, observed phenomenon in heteroxenous parasites (Poulin, 1994; Lafferty, 1999). By directly or indirectly enacting a change to the host, the parasite can increase the likelihood of its transmission to the following host by inducing a higher risk of predation to the host (Poulin, 1994; Lafferty, 1999). While many doubts around this process still exist, the large number of examples in its support cannot be ignored (Heil, 2016). Box 1: A collection of applicable terms with which to describe a parasite Endoparasite: Lives internally in the host, in contact with host homoeostasis. Ectoparasite: Lives externally on the host, in contact with the outside environment. Monoxenous (direct) parasite: One host species required for full development. Heteroxenous (indirect) parasite: Multiple host species required for full development. Facultative parasite: Does not require a host to complete the life cycle, but can be parasitic. Obligate parasite: Requires host to complete life cycle. Partial parasite: Life cycle is a combination of parasitic and free-living stages. Total parasite: No free-living stages in life cycle. Host-parasite interactions that drive metabolic responses in infected fish are rooted in the parasitic mussel’s attachment strategy and its effects on host tissue physiology. Freshwater mussels rely on an obligate parasitic larval stage, the glochidia, which must attach to fish hosts to complete development and can disrupt native host-parasite interactions [N1-R1]. Glochidia attach to the gills or fins of fishes and exhibit varying degrees of host specificity, which implies that the initial interaction is highly structured and species-dependent [N1-R2]. The parasitic larval stage becomes encysted in host tissue, eventually excysting to develop into a free-living adult [N2-F1]. This attachment and encystment process is likely a key driver of host tissue disruption, because the review notes that host fish compensate through rapid wound healing in parasitized areas and higher ventilation rates [N2-F1].

The evidence points to several organs and metabolic pathways that are most affected. The review emphasizes that mussels cause minor effects on hosts, typically only observable in combination with other stressors, and that the most visible effects are on metabolic rate and behavior indicative of stress [N2-F1]. It also notes that studies on host metabolic activity show mixed but mostly negative short-term effects on host oxygen consumption, muscle activity, and ammonia excretion [N2-R1]. These findings suggest that the metabolic response is broad but not uniform: the main affected systems appear to be aerobic metabolism, locomotor activity, and excretory function, with ammonia excretion being a key indicator of altered metabolic load [N2-R1]. The review also connects these effects to increases in metabolic rate and behavior indicative of stress, supporting the idea that metabolic responses are part of a broader physiological stress response rather than a single pathway [N2-F1].

On the question of whether host defenses or resource diversion are the main mechanism, the evidence is mixed but leans toward both. The review says that host fish compensate through rapid wound healing and higher ventilation rates [N2-F1]. That is a classic defensive response, indicating host effort to repair tissue damage and improve gas exchange. At the same time, the negative effects on metabolic rate and behavior suggest that parasitism may also divert resources from normal physiological function, as the host appears to be paying a metabolic price for the parasite’s presence [N2-R1]. The review also states that the range of effect intensities varies greatly with the species involved, which implies that both host-specific defenses and species-specific parasite biology contribute to the overall metabolic outcome [N2-F1]. The evidence does not strongly distinguish one mechanism as dominant over the other, but it does support a dual model in which tissue repair and resource diversion interact with stress-related metabolic changes [N2-F1; N2-R1].

Mussel species differences shape host metabolic outcomes because mussel biology varies in parasitism strategy, host specificity, and life-history traits. The review notes that freshwater mussels in the order Unionida are highly adapted to parasitize fish for dispersal, with glochidia attaching to gills or fins and becoming encysted in host tissue [N2-F1]. It also states that glochidia exhibit varying degrees of host specificity [N1-R2], which means that different mussel species may impose different physiological demands on fish hosts. The review further notes that the effects caused by infestation may play a role in normal functioning of the host immune system or physiological processes, and that species differences in the interaction may arise from different evolutionary strategies between long- and short-infesting mussels [N2-F1]. This is a key point for explaining species differences: some mussels may have evolved more prolonged or less prolonged parasitic phases, which could alter how much host tissue is occupied, how long the host is stressed, and how much energy is diverted from growth or other functions [N2-F1].

The most studied mussel species in the provided evidence are those that are ecologically prominent and experimentally tractable. Margaritifera margaritifera is especially emphasized as a unique mussel, though the review warns that conclusions drawn from it may not generalize well across species [N2-F1]. The review also references studies on the effects of parasitic freshwater mussels on host fishes that are used to establish host specificity and preference of mussel species to host fishes [N1-R3]. In addition, the study on brown trout infested with glochidia from Margaritifera margaritifera is directly relevant, showing that parasitized trout had significantly lower specific growth rate than non-infested trout, even though survival was similar [N4-F2]. This species combination is therefore a strong example of species-specific impact: the same mussel species can produce measurable metabolic effects in a host species, but the magnitude depends on the host [N4-F2].

The evidence for species-specific effects on growth, survival, or reproduction is strongest for growth. The review notes that lower growth and reduced osmotic potential in infested hosts are commonly observed and correlated with infestation load [N2-F1]. The brown trout study found that parasitized trout had significantly lower specific growth rate than non-infested trout, but survival was not reduced [N4-F2]. The evidence for survival is therefore more mixed: some studies show no survival effect, while others imply that heavy infestation may become harmful when combined with other stressors [N2-F1]. For reproduction, the provided evidence is thinner, but the review’s broader emphasis on mussel-host interactions shaping ecological and evolutionary dynamics suggests that reproductive effects are plausible in longer-term or more intense parasitism scenarios [N2-F1].

Possible explanations for species differences in host impact include life-history strategy, host specificity, and the length of the parasitic phase. The review explicitly mentions that species differences may arise from different evolutionary strategies between long- and short-infesting mussels [N2-F1]. It also notes that mussel species may differ in host compatibility, with one study showing that A. anatina had higher infestation rates and excystment rates than another species, and different host compatibility [N3-R2]. This implies that some mussel species are better adapted to specific host physiology, which can affect how quickly or severely they impair host function. The brown trout study also shows that parasitic larvae can induce upstream movement and habitat use changes, which may reflect a species-specific manipulation of host behavior [N4-F2]. Taken together, these explanations suggest that mussel species differences shape host metabolic outcomes through a combination of attachment biology, host compatibility, parasitism duration, and ecological manipulation [N1-R2; N2-F1; N3-R2; N4-F2].

## Integrated synthesis: How freshwater fish metabolic responses vary by mussel load and species

Freshwater fish metabolic responses to parasitic freshwater mussels vary in a way that is shaped by both the species of mussel and the load of infection. The evidence suggests a recurring pattern: parasitic mussels generally impose a mild but measurable metabolic burden on hosts, often with trade-offs between growth, condition, and survival, while the exact magnitude and direction of the effect depend on which mussel species is involved and how many glochidia are present [N2-F1; N4-F2]. The synthesis below is organized around the central question: **what combinations show strong metabolic trade-offs, where responses are consistent across studies, and where findings are conflicting or inconclusive**; and how **host-specific physiology** explains these differences.

---

## 1) How mussels drive metabolic responses in infected fish

The metabolic response begins with the host-parasite interaction itself. Freshwater mussels rely on an obligate parasitic larval stage, the glochidia, which must attach to fish hosts to complete development [N1-R1]. Glochidia attach to the gills or fins of fishes and exhibit varying degrees of host specificity [N1-R2]. Once attached, they encyst in host tissue and eventually excyst to develop into free-living adults [N2-F1]. This attachment and encystment process is the primary mechanism through which mussels disrupt host physiology.

The evidence indicates that the most affected host organs and metabolic pathways are those involved in gas exchange, locomotion, and excretion. The review states that host fish compensate through rapid wound healing in parasitized areas and higher ventilation rates [N2-F1]. It also notes that studies on host metabolic activity show mixed but mostly negative short-term effects on oxygen consumption, muscle activity, and ammonia excretion [N2-R1]. These findings suggest that the metabolic response is broad but not uniform: the main affected systems appear to be aerobic metabolism, locomotor activity, and excretory function, with ammonia excretion being a key indicator of altered metabolic load [N2-R1].

The mechanism is likely a combination of host defenses and resource diversion. Host fish compensate through wound healing and ventilation, which are defensive responses [N2-F1]. At the same time, parasitism appears to divert resources from normal physiological function, as the host pays a metabolic price for the parasite’s presence [N2-R1]. The review also emphasizes that the range of effect intensities varies greatly with the species involved, implying that both host-specific defenses and species-specific parasite biology contribute to the overall metabolic outcome [N2-F1]. In other words, the response is not simply a single mechanism; it is a dynamic interaction between tissue repair, metabolic stress, and resource allocation.

---

## 2) How mussel species differences shape host metabolic outcomes

Mussel species differences shape host metabolic outcomes because mussel biology varies in parasitism strategy, host specificity, and life-history traits. The review notes that freshwater mussels in the order Unionida are highly adapted to parasitize fish for dispersal, with glochidia attaching to gills or fins and becoming encysted in host tissue [N2-F1]. It also states that glochidia exhibit varying degrees of host specificity [N1-R2], which means that different mussel species may impose different physiological demands on fish hosts.

The most studied mussel species in the evidence are those that are ecologically prominent and experimentally tractable. Margaritifera margaritifera is especially emphasized as a unique mussel, though the review warns that conclusions drawn from it may not generalize well across species [N2-F1]. The review also references studies on the effects of parasitic freshwater mussels on host fishes that are used to establish host specificity and preference of mussel species to host fishes [N1-R3]. In addition, the study on brown trout infested with glochidia from Margaritifera margaritifera is directly relevant, showing that parasitized trout had significantly lower specific growth rate than non-infested trout, even though survival was not reduced [N4-F2]. This species combination is therefore a strong example of species-specific impact: the same mussel species can produce measurable metabolic effects in a host species, but the magnitude depends on the host [N4-F2].

The evidence for species-specific effects is strongest for growth. The review notes that lower growth and reduced osmotic potential in infested hosts are commonly observed and correlated with infestation load [N2-F1]. The brown trout study shows that parasitized trout had significantly lower specific growth rate than non-infested trout, but survival was not reduced [N4-F2]. The evidence for survival is therefore more mixed: some studies show no survival effect, while others imply that heavy infestation may become harmful when combined with other stressors [N2-F1]. For reproduction, the provided evidence is thinner, but the broader emphasis on mussel-host interactions shaping ecological and evolutionary dynamics suggests that reproductive effects are plausible in longer-term or more intense parasitism scenarios [N2-F1].

Possible explanations for species differences in host impact include life-history strategy, host specificity, and the length of the parasitic phase. The review explicitly mentions that species differences may arise from different evolutionary strategies between long- and short-infesting mussels [N2-F1]. It also notes that mussel species may differ in host compatibility, with one study showing that A. anatina had higher infestation rates and excystment rates than another species, and different host compatibility [N3-R2]. This implies that some mussel species are better adapted to specific host physiology, which can affect how quickly or severely they impair host function. The brown trout study also shows that parasitic larvae can induce upstream movement and habitat use changes, which may reflect a species-specific manipulation of host behavior [N4-F2]. Taken together, these explanations suggest that mussel species differences shape host metabolic outcomes through a combination of attachment biology, host compatibility, parasitism duration, and ecological manipulation [N1-R2; N2-F1; N3-R2; N4-F2].

## 3) How parasite load affects fish metabolic responses

Parasite load affects fish metabolic responses in a way that is often nonlinear, with load thresholds and host condition or species moderating the outcome. The evidence shows that lower growth and reduced osmotic potential in infested hosts are commonly observed and correlated with infestation load [N2-F1]. This indicates that metabolic and physiological effects do not appear to be uniform across all parasite loads; instead, they increase with load, at least up to a point. ## 4) Variation across mussel-host combinations

## 5) Host-specific physiology moderates metabolic responses

Host-specific physiology appears to moderate metabolic responses to parasitic mussels in at least three ways: fish species differences, condition-dependent trade-offs, and life-history strategy. ---

## 6) Integrated conclusion

In short, freshwater fish metabolic responses to parasitic freshwater mussels vary by load and species in a pattern that is often nonlinear and moderated by host physiology. At the same time, the evidence is uneven: some combinations show strong metabolic trade-offs, such as the brown trout–Margaritifera margaritifera example; responses are consistent across studies in showing a generally negative impact on growth and metabolic activity; and findings are conflicting or inconclusive for many combinations [N2-F1; N2-R1; N4-F2]. - **Evidence is uneven:** The clearest strong trade-offs are in well-studied combinations; for many other combinations, the evidence is thin or mixed [N2-F1; N4-F2].

Instead, it is a complex interaction in which the species of mussel, the number of parasites, and the physiological state of the host all shape whether the fish pays a metabolic price, how large that price is, and whether the price is paid in growth, survival, or behavior [N2-F1; N4-F2; N6-R2].
